column1: # Settings of the edge image: the single source of truth for their defaults, the start-up check and SECURITY: summary
# (docker-entrypoint.d/05-kickedro-settings.envsh), the variables the templates may use (18-kickedro-render.sh), and
# One setting per line: seven fields separated by one TAB each, none empty or blank (a line that is not exactly so
# stops the container, and the docs generator). Lines starting with "#" and empty lines are ignored.
#   DEFAULT      value used when the variable is unset or empty
#   ALLOWED      accepted values: alternatives separated by "|", each a literal value or one of these forms:
#                  <integer>  a whole number from 1, at most 15 digits
#                  <time>     a whole number from 1, at most 9 digits, with the unit ms, s, m or h, e.g. 10s
#                  <buffers>  a count (1 to 4 digits) and a size of at least 1k separated by one space, e.g. 4 8k;
#                             the size in bytes or with k or m, at most 7 digits
#                  <path>     an absolute file path (letters, digits and . _ / - only)
#                  <methods>  HTTP methods separated by single spaces, each of capital letters and -, starting with a
#                             letter (at most 32 characters), e.g. GET HEAD POST OPTIONS PUT
#                  <content-types>  |type/subtype| items separated by single spaces, in lower case: letters, digits
#                             and . + _ -, each part starting with a letter or digit, e.g. |application/json| |text/plain|
#                  <headers>  /name/ items separated by single spaces: header names in lower case, letters, digits
#                             and -, starting with a letter or digit (at most 64 characters), e.g. /proxy/ /if/
#                  (a list has 1 to 100 items and at most 2000 characters)
#   WEAKER_IF    which values are weaker than the default; each prints one SECURITY: line at start:
#                  -          none (no value is less secure than another)
#                  >X         a value above X: numbers by value, times by duration, buffers when the count or the
#                  +          a list with an item that the default list does not have (it allows more)
#                  <          a list without an item of the default list (it restricts less)
#   RISK_TEXT    the protection lost by weakening (the SECURITY: line, and "If you weaken it" in the docs)
#   WHEN         when you might change it (docs)

column5: Attacks are no longer blocked: DetectionOnly only logs them, Off does not even inspect requests.
column6: ModSecurity's rule engine: On inspects requests and blocks attacks, DetectionOnly inspects and logs only, Off switches the WAF off.
column7: DetectionOnly for a first period on a new site, to find false positives in the audit log before blocking.

column5: No weaker value: 1 is the lowest level. Higher levels block more attacks and cause more false positives.
column6: OWASP CRS blocking paranoia level: how many and how strict the rules that block are.
column7: Raise it for sites that handle sensitive data, after adding exclusions for the extra false positives.

column5: A request must match more rules before it is blocked, so attacks that match only one or two rules get through.
column6: OWASP CRS inbound anomaly score threshold: a request is blocked when its matched rules add up to this score (one critical match scores 5).
column7: Briefly, while tuning a site with many false positives; narrow exclusions in custom.d are better.

column5: Responses that leak data (error messages, source code, directory listings) must match more rules before they are blocked.
column6: OWASP CRS outbound anomaly score threshold for responses.
column7: When normal responses of an application match outbound rules that cannot be excluded narrowly.

column5: Larger request bodies are accepted and buffered for inspection, which costs memory and disk and eases denial of service.
column6: Largest request body, file uploads included, in bytes (default 128 MiB); a larger body is refused.
column7: Raise it for sites that take larger uploads; lower it for sites that never do.

column5: Larger form, JSON and XML bodies are buffered and parsed for inspection, which costs memory and CPU per request and eases denial of service.
column6: Largest request body without its file uploads (form fields, JSON, XML), in bytes; a larger one is refused with MODSEC_DENY_STATUS and the block page. The default, 1 MiB, is nginx's own default client_max_body_size, so with nginx's defaults the WAF never refuses a body that nginx accepts (ModSecurity's recommended value is 128 KiB). MODSEC_REQ_BODY_LIMIT caps the whole body, files included.
column7: Raise it together with client_max_body_size for applications that send larger forms or JSON documents. Tighten it (131072 is ModSecurity's recommended value) where no application needs large bodies: each request can then make the WAF buffer and parse less.

column5: Requests with more arguments are parsed and inspected in full, which costs CPU per request and eases denial of service.
column6: Most arguments (query string and form fields together) a request may have: one with this many or more is refused with MODSEC_DENY_STATUS and the block page (rule 200007), because ModSecurity would not inspect the arguments beyond it. The default, 3000, fits large admin forms such as WordPress menus with many items (ModSecurity's recommended value is 1000).
column7: Raise it for even larger forms (PHP's max_input_vars is the same kind of limit). Tighten it (1000 is ModSecurity's value) where no form is that large: each request can then make the WAF parse less.

column2: GET HEAD POST OPTIONS PUT PATCH DELETE
column5: Requests with the added methods are no longer refused by policy, so applications get methods they may not expect (WebDAV methods and others) and more of what they offer is reachable.
column6: HTTP methods the OWASP CRS allows (its tx.allowed_methods); a request with another method is refused (rule 911100). The default is the CRS's own list, GET HEAD POST OPTIONS, plus PUT PATCH DELETE, which REST APIs and single-page applications use.
column7: Tighten it to GET HEAD POST OPTIONS where no application uses PUT, PATCH or DELETE: such requests are then refused before they reach an application that might act on them. Add the WebDAV methods (PROPFIND, MKCOL, ...) for WebDAV, CalDAV or Nextcloud. See docs/configuration.md.

column5: Request bodies of the added types are accepted, but ModSecurity parses only forms, multipart, XML and JSON: the content of other types reaches applications with much less inspection, so an attack gets through by naming such a type.
column6: Request body content types the OWASP CRS allows (its tx.allowed_request_content_type), each between bars; a request with another type is refused (rule 920420). The CRS also allows application/*+json and two AWS JSON types by itself. The default is the CRS's own list, on purpose: it refuses raw-file uploads (application/octet-stream: WebDAV, file sync, container registries), text/plain beacons and CSP reports.
column7: Add a type only for the sites that receive it, best with a one-line custom.d rule for those hosts (see docs/configuration.md); this setting adds it for every site, so give the whole list.

column5: Requests with the request headers left out of the list are no longer refused, although the OWASP CRS lists them as known risks: Content-Encoding hides a compressed body from inspection, Proxy is the httpoxy attack, X-Middleware-Subrequest bypasses Next.js middleware (CVE-2025-29927).
column6: Request headers the OWASP CRS refuses (its tx.restricted_headers_basic, rule 920450), each between slashes. The default is the CRS's own list without the method-override headers (X-HTTP-Method-Override, X-HTTP-Method, X-Method-Override; WordPress's block editor sends the first) and without Expect (curl and .NET clients send it with uploads; nginx answers it itself and does not forward it to backends it proxies to, as nginx-proxy does for HTTP and HTTPS backends).
column7: Tighten it with /x-http-method-override/ /x-http-method/ /x-method-override/ where no application needs a method override: an application then cannot be made to act on a method the WAF did not see. Adding /expect/ restores the CRS's full list. See docs/configuration.md.

column5: Blocked and suspicious requests are no longer recorded: no trace of attacks, and block page references cannot be looked up.
column6: Where ModSecurity writes its audit log (blocked requests and other relevant transactions): a file, /dev/stdout (in docker logs), or off.
column7: A file on a mounted, rotated volume when docker logs are not kept or are hard to parse.

column5: No security effect: both formats record the same transactions.
column6: Audit log format: one JSON object per transaction, or ModSecurity's native multi-part format.
column7: Native when your log tooling expects it.

column5: No security effect: every allowed status refuses the request. With 444 nginx closes the connection without a response, so there is no block page.
column6: HTTP status of the response to a request ModSecurity refuses: one the OWASP CRS blocks, and one the request body checks refuse (rules 200002 to 200007: a body over MODSEC_REQ_BODY_NOFILES_LIMIT, MODSEC_ARGUMENTS_LIMIT arguments or more, a body that cannot be parsed, an internal error such as a regular-expression limit). A body over MODSEC_REQ_BODY_LIMIT is refused by ModSecurity itself, always with 403. Rules of your own set their own status.
column7: To match what clients or monitoring expect, or 444 to send scanners nothing at all.

column5: The exact nginx version appears in the Server header and on error pages, which helps attackers pick known vulnerabilities.
column6: Whether the nginx version appears in the Server header and on nginx's error pages (nginx's server_tokens).
column7: For debugging only.

column5: The X-Powered-By, Server, X-AspNet-Version and X-AspNetMvc-Version headers of backends reach clients and reveal their software and versions.
column6: Removes X-Powered-By, Server, X-AspNet-Version and X-AspNetMvc-Version from backend responses (proxied, FastCGI, uWSGI and gRPC). A vhost snippet that sets its own proxy_hide_header or proxy_pass_header (or the FastCGI, uWSGI or gRPC one) replaces this list where it is set.
column7: When a client depends on one of these headers.

column5: Responses lose X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy and X-Frame-Options: MIME sniffing, full URLs in referrers to other sites, and clickjacking through frames become possible again.
column6: Adds X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin and X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN to every response, error pages included, unless it already has that header (from the backend or the vhost). Also on vhosts that add headers of their own (HSTS), through nginx's add_header_inherit merge; a vhost snippet that sets add_header_inherit off or on loses them where it is set.
column7: When all applications send these headers themselves and you want nginx's stock add_header inheritance.

column5: Clients may take longer to send the request headers, so slow-header attacks (Slowloris) hold connections longer.
column6: Time a client has to send the complete request line and headers.
column7: For clients on very slow or unreliable links.

column5: Clients may pause longer while sending a request body, so slow-body attacks hold connections longer.
column6: Longest pause between two reads of the request body (not the time for the whole upload).
column7: For uploads over very slow or unreliable links.

column5: Clients that read responses very slowly hold connections and buffers longer.
column6: Longest pause between two writes of the response to the client (not the time for the whole download).
column7: For clients on very slow or unreliable links.

column5: Idle keep-alive connections stay open longer and take connection slots that an attacker can exhaust.
column6: How long an idle keep-alive connection stays open; 0 disables keep-alive.
column7: For clients that make requests with long pauses in between, such as a load balancer that reuses connections.

column5: Longer request lines and headers are accepted, which costs memory per connection and eases denial of service.
column6: Number and size of the buffers for long request lines and headers; a longer request line or header field is refused (414 or 400).
column7: When an application uses very long URLs or very large cookies.

column5: No security effect: with off, nginx's plain error page is sent, without a reference. Neither page shows rule details.
column6: A request ModSecurity blocks gets a short page with a reference: the request ID, which is also the transaction ID of its audit log entry. Other error pages nginx itself sends with the deny status (for example for deny rules) get it too; pages from backends never do. A vhost snippet with a sub_filter of its own gets nginx's plain page instead. A file mounted at /etc/nginx/kickedro/block-page.html (at most 32 KiB) replaces the built-in page; {{request_id}} in it is replaced by the reference. With the page on, the image also sets nginx's msie_padding off for the whole server (otherwise nginx appends padding comments for MSIE and Chrome to short error pages, the block page included), unless a conf.d file sets msie_padding itself.
column7: Off when the clients are programs that do not show pages.

column5: No security effect by itself: the zones limit nothing until a vhost uses them, and a vhost that uses them stops nginx from starting when they are off.
column6: Defines the rate-limit zones kickedro_perip_10rs (10 requests per second per client address) and kickedro_login_1rs (1 per second) for limit_req in vhost snippets; applied nowhere by default.
column7: Off to save their shared memory (10 MB each) when no vhost uses them.
